props.title: Dracula

sections.content: Tod Browning's Dracula revolutionized horror cinema, establishing Universal's monster movie golden age and cementing Bela Lugosi's iconic portrayal as the definitive vampire count. The film's Gothic atmosphere, achieved through Charles D. Hall's elaborate castle sets and Karl Freund's expressionistic cinematography, created a template that horror films would follow for decades. While earlier vampire films like Nosferatu (1922) took a more grotesque approach, Lugosi's sophisticated, seductive Dracula transformed the vampire into a charismatic aristocrat - a characterization that influenced everything from Horror of Dracula (1958) to Interview with the Vampire (1994).

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond vampire movies. Its blend of horror and sophistication paved the way for psychological thrillers like Cat People (1942) and The Innocents (1961). Lugosi's performance - with his hypnotic stare and precise, theatrical movements - created a new type of screen villain: the monster as aristocrat. This characterization influenced countless subsequent performances, from Vincent Price in House of Usher (1960) to Anthony Hopkins in The Silence of the Lambs (1991).

The technical innovations in Dracula were groundbreaking for their time. Cinematographer Karl Freund, fresh from German Expressionist masterpieces, brought a shadowy, atmospheric style that would define Universal horror. His techniques - particularly the use of strategically placed lights to illuminate Lugosi's eyes - became standard horror practice. These methods influenced film noir of the 1940s and can be seen in modern Gothic works like Crimson Peak (2015) and The Woman in Black (2012). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Modern Interpretations

sections.content: The film's impact on vampire mythology cannot be overstated. While Bram Stoker's novel provided the foundation, Dracula created many of the visual and dramatic conventions we now associate with vampires. The formal evening wear, the aristocratic manner, the Old World charm masking predatory intent - these elements influenced everything from Dark Shadows (1966-1971) to Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992). Even subversive takes like Near Dark (1987) and Only Lovers Left Alive (2013) define themselves in opposition to the Lugosi archetype.
